name: Scalping
definition: An ultra-short-horizon trading style in which a trader opens and closes positions within seconds to minutes to capture very small price movements, often exploiting the bid-ask spread or momentary micro-imbalances in highly liquid instruments. It is the shortest-horizon form of day trading and relies on high trade frequency, tight risk limits, and low per-trade costs.
intuition: Instead of trying to catch a big move, the scalper skims many tiny moves, accepting a few ticks of profit per trade and repeating this dozens or hundreds of times a day.
mechanics: Positions are established and liquidated within minutes or seconds, using direct-access execution, level-2/order-book data, and strict stop discipline. Profit per trade is typically a fraction of a percent, so commissions, fees, and slippage must be minimized; small losses are cut immediately because a single large loss can erase dozens of wins.
failure_modes: Transaction costs and slippage can exceed the small gross edge; during volatility spikes or thin liquidity, stops are jumped and small losses become large ones.
misconceptions: That scalping is easy money because each trade is small and quick; in practice most retail scalpers lose after costs, and the SEC warns that day traders typically suffer severe financial losses. Scalping is also confused with the illegal practice of 'scalping' by advisers who tout a stock after secretly buying it.
example: A trader buys 2,000 shares of a liquid large-cap stock at $50.01 and sells them seconds later at $50.04, capturing about $60 gross before fees, repeating the process many times per session.

name: Day trading
definition: A speculative trading approach in which a trader buys and sells (or sells and buys) the same financial instrument within the same trading day, closing all positions before the session ends to avoid overnight gap risk. Under FINRA rules, a 'day trade' is the purchase and sale of the same security on the same day in a margin account, and customers executing four or more day trades in five business days are designated pattern day traders subject to special margin requirements.
intuition: Day traders try to profit from intraday price swings, riding a stock's momentum for seconds to hours, and never hold positions overnight.
mechanics: Positions are opened and closed during a single session, often on margin and with direct-access platforms; true day traders hold nothing overnight. In U.S. margin accounts, pattern day traders must maintain at least $25,000 in equity and are subject to day-trading buying-power limits.
failure_modes: High leverage, commissions, and spread costs cause most retail day traders to lose money; academic studies of day traders find that the large majority are unprofitable after fees.
misconceptions: That day trading is a form of investing or a reliable income source; the SEC states that day traders do not 'invest', typically suffer severe losses in their first months, and should never risk money needed for living expenses or retirement.
example: A trader buys 500 shares of XYZ at $41.20 at 10:00 a.m. after a breakout, sells them at $41.75 by 11:30 a.m., and holds no position into the close.

name: Swing trading
definition: A speculative trading style in which positions are held for one or more days up to several weeks to profit from short- to medium-term price 'swings'. Holding periods sit between day trading (closed intraday) and position trading or buy-and-hold (months to years), and entries/exits are typically driven by technical analysis, sometimes combined with fundamentals.
intuition: The swing trader tries to catch the middle chunk of a move that plays out over days, without needing to buy the exact bottom or sell the exact top.
mechanics: Traders identify setups (trend continuation, pullbacks to support, breakouts) on daily or intraday charts, enter with predefined stops and targets, and hold overnight, accepting gap risk in exchange for capturing multi-day moves. Rule-based swing systems encode entry/exit as objective technical rules.
failure_modes: Overnight and weekend gaps can blow through stops; in choppy, trendless markets swing signals whipsaw and repeated small losses accumulate.
misconceptions: That swing trading reliably times tops and bottoms, or that widely followed rule-based setups keep their edge; competition and regime change erode simple swing rules.
example: A trader buys a stock pulling back to its rising 20-day average at $88, places a stop at $85 and a target at $96, and exits eight trading days later.

name: Position trading
definition: A trading style in which positions are held for weeks to months (or longer) to capture major price trends, with decisions driven mainly by macro trends, fundamentals, or long-horizon technical analysis. The term is sometimes used interchangeably with buy and hold, though position traders may actively exit when the underlying thesis or long-term trend ends.
intuition: Position traders ignore daily noise and try to own an asset for the big part of a long move, reviewing the thesis periodically rather than watching the tape.
mechanics: Entries are based on long-term trend signals (e.g., weekly charts, macro or fundamental theses); stops are wide and positions are reviewed weekly or monthly rather than intraday. Transaction costs are low because turnover is low, but capital is exposed to drawdowns over long holding periods.
failure_modes: Wide stops mean large per-trade losses when a long-term thesis is wrong; secular reversals or value traps can hold capital in losing positions for years.
misconceptions: That position trading is identical to passive buy-and-hold indexing; position traders actively select securities and exit when trends or theses fail, whereas buy and hold implies no market timing at all.
example: A trader goes long an equity index ETF after a weekly golden cross, holds for nine months through interim corrections, and exits when the weekly trend breaks.

name: Trend following
definition: A systematic trading approach that takes long positions in instruments whose own recent returns have been positive and short positions in those whose recent returns have been negative, on the hypothesis that price trends persist. It is an empirical strategy family, not a proven predictive law; academic work documents that a security's own past returns positively predict its near-term future returns across many futures markets, with partial reversal at longer horizons.
intuition: Rather than predicting turning points, trend followers assume a market that has been going up will keep going up for a while, and they ride it until the trend reverses.
mechanics: Signals are computed from past returns or price series (e.g., sign of the trailing 12-month excess return, moving-average filters, channel breakouts); positions are often scaled by inverse volatility and diversified across equity index, bond, currency, and commodity futures. Positions are exited or flipped when the trend signal reverses.
formula: Position sign s_t = sign(r_{t-12,t}), where r_{t-12,t} is the instrument's excess return over the past 12 months (Moskowitz, Ooi, Pedersen 2012); position size is commonly scaled as s_t / sigma_t with sigma_t an ex-ante volatility estimate.
failure_modes: In range-bound or mean-reverting markets trend signals whipsaw, producing strings of small losses; trend strategies also suffer sharp drawdowns at abrupt trend reversals (e.g., V-shaped recoveries).
misconceptions: That trend following predicts where prices will go; it is purely reactive to what prices have done and its documented edge is a statistical regularity that can weaken as it is crowded, not a guarantee.
example: A CTA goes long S&P 500 futures because the 12-month return is positive, sizes the position to 10% annualized volatility, and flips short a year later after the trailing return turns negative.

name: Mean reversion
definition: The hypothesis, and the family of strategies built on it, that asset prices or returns contain a transitory component that tends to revert toward a long-run mean, so that extreme moves are at least partially undone. Empirically, stock returns show positive serial correlation at short horizons and negative autocorrelation at long horizons, consistent with a slowly decaying transitory price component, though the effect is statistical and contested, not a law.
intuition: What stretches too far from its usual level tends to snap back; mean-reversion traders buy what has fallen too far and sell what has risen too far.
mechanics: Traders measure deviation from an estimated mean (moving average, fair-value model, or historical spread) and take positions expecting reversion, exiting when the series returns toward its mean. Statistically, mean reversion is tested with variance-ratio tests or modeled with mean-reverting processes such as Ornstein-Uhlenbeck.
formula: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model: dX_t = theta * (mu - X_t) dt + sigma dW_t, where mu is the long-run mean, theta the speed of reversion, and sigma the volatility; variance-ratio test: VR(q) = Var(r_t^q) / (q * Var(r_t)), with VR < 1 indicating mean reversion (Poterba and Summers 1988).
failure_modes: When the underlying equilibrium shifts (structural breaks, bankruptcies, regime change), 'cheap' assets keep getting cheaper; betting against strong trends produces large losses, and estimated reversion speeds are unstable out of sample.
misconceptions: That prices must revert to a historical mean on a predictable schedule, or that mean reversion contradicts momentum; empirically both coexist at different horizons, and apparent reversion can reflect time-varying required returns rather than mispricing.
example: A stock drops 12% in two weeks on no fundamental news while its sector is flat; a mean-reversion trader buys, expecting the gap versus its 60-day average to close, and exits after an 8% rebound.

name: Momentum trading
definition: A family of strategies that buy assets with strong recent performance and sell or short assets with weak recent performance, based on the empirically documented pattern that securities outperforming their peers over the past 3 to 12 months tend to keep outperforming over the following month. Momentum is a well-studied cross-sectional anomaly, not a guaranteed law, and is distinct from time-series momentum, which uses an asset's own past return rather than its rank versus peers.
intuition: Winners tend to keep winning for a while, so the momentum trader buys what is already strong and avoids or shorts what is weak.
mechanics: Universe securities are ranked on trailing (typically 3- to 12-month) returns, skipping the most recent month to avoid short-term reversal; the portfolio goes long the top decile/quintile and short the bottom, rebalanced periodically. Retail implementations simply buy instruments breaking to new highs or showing high relative strength.
formula: Momentum score M_i = R_i(t-12, t-1), the cumulative return of asset i from 12 months to 1 month before formation; portfolios are formed by sorting on M (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993).
failure_modes: Momentum crashes occur at sharp market reversals (e.g., 2009), when past losers rebound violently and the short leg surges; crowding and transaction costs also erode the gross anomaly.
misconceptions: That momentum means simply chasing whatever is up; systematic momentum is a ranked, hedged, periodically rebalanced portfolio construction, and its long-run returns come with occasional severe crashes.
example: Each month a quant ranks 500 stocks on their trailing 6-month return, buys the top 30, shorts the bottom 30, and rebalances monthly.

name: Breakout trading
definition: A technical-analysis trading style that enters a position when price passes through and holds beyond a defined support or resistance level, on the hypothesis that such breakouts mark the early stage of a new trend. It is an analytical framework, not a proven predictive law; broken resistance is often treated as new support and vice versa.
intuition: When price finally escapes the ceiling or floor where it has been stuck, breakout traders jump in, betting the escape is the start of a real move.
mechanics: Traders mark horizontal support/resistance from prior swing highs and lows, then place buy stops above resistance or sell stops below support, often confirming with volume. Stops are placed back inside the broken level (a breakout that immediately re-enters the range is treated as failed).
formula: Typical long trigger: enter if P_t > R, where R = max(High_{t-N}, ..., High_{t-1}) over a chosen lookback N; stop placed at or below R after entry.
failure_modes: False breakouts are common, especially in low-volume or range-bound conditions: price pokes through the level, triggers entries, then reverses back into the range, stopping out breakout traders repeatedly.
misconceptions: That a breakout predicts continued movement with high probability; support/resistance levels are heuristic constructs, and the frequency of failed breakouts means risk control, not prediction, drives any edge.
example: A stock has failed three times near $60; a trader places a buy stop at $60.25 with volume confirmation and a protective stop at $58.50 when filled.

name: Range trading
definition: A trading style applied to non-trending markets in which price repeatedly rises off a support level and falls off a resistance level; the trader buys near support and sells or shorts near resistance, expecting the oscillation to persist. It is a technical-analysis heuristic whose validity ends when the range breaks.
intuition: If a stock keeps bouncing between the same floor and ceiling, trade the bounce: buy low in the band, sell high in the band.
mechanics: Support and resistance are identified from repeated reaction highs/lows; entries are taken near the boundaries with stops just outside the range and targets near the opposite boundary. Oscillators (e.g., stochastic, RSI) are often used to time entries within the range.
failure_modes: The strategy is destroyed by range breakouts: a position entered at the 'wrong' boundary just before a genuine breakout loses continuously, and repeated range profits can be erased by one failed range.
misconceptions: That ranges are stable structures; what looks like a range is often just a pause in a trend, and the edges are fuzzy zones rather than precise prices.
example: EUR/USD oscillates between 1.0800 and 1.1000 for two months; a range trader buys near 1.0820 with a stop at 1.0770 and a target at 1.0970.

name: Pairs trading
definition: A market-neutral strategy that matches two securities whose prices historically move together, then goes long the underperformer and short the outperformer when their prices diverge, profiting if the spread between them reconverges. Gatev, Goetzmann, and Rouwenhorst (2006) formalized the canonical version: stocks are paired by minimum distance between normalized historical prices and traded with a simple divergence/convergence rule.
intuition: If two similar companies' prices drift apart, bet they will come back together: buy the laggard, short the leader, and you profit on the gap closing regardless of market direction.
mechanics: Pairs are formed from a historical estimation window (e.g., 12 months of normalized prices or a cointegration/hedge-ratio regression); a trade opens when the spread widens beyond a threshold (e.g., two standard deviations) and closes on convergence or at the end of a fixed horizon. Dollar-neutral sizing makes the position roughly insensitive to market moves.
formula: Spread S_t = ln P_A,t - beta * ln P_B,t, where beta is the hedge ratio from regressing A's log price on B's; trade when z_t = (S_t - mu_S) / sigma_S exceeds an entry band (commonly +/-2), exit when z_t crosses 0.
failure_modes: When the historical co-movement breaks for fundamental reasons (e.g., one firm is deteriorating), the spread widens instead of converging; pairs profits also decayed after the strategy became crowded in the 2000s.
misconceptions: That a diverging pair must reconverge because it always did before; co-movement is a statistical association that can break permanently, so divergence can signal a real relative-value change rather than a temporary mispricing.
example: Coca-Cola and PepsiCo normalized prices diverge by 2.5 standard deviations; the trader shorts the outperformer and buys the underperformer in equal dollar amounts, exiting when the spread returns to its mean.

name: Statistical arbitrage
definition: A family of quantitative, typically market-neutral strategies that exploit statistical mispricings among large portfolios of related securities, using short-horizon mean reversion and factor models rather than the strict riskless mispricing of classical arbitrage. Pairs trading is the canonical example; profits are expected values over many small trades, not risk-free arbitrage.
intuition: Instead of one guaranteed mispricing, stat arb places hundreds of small, hedged bets that each have a slight statistical edge, so the law of large numbers does the work.
mechanics: Models estimate expected short-horizon returns from residuals after removing factor exposures; portfolios are built long undervalued and short overvalued securities, neutralized to market and common factors, and turned over quickly. Gatev et al. (2006) link pairs-trading profits to temporary mispricing of close substitutes with a common return factor.
failure_modes: Model risk and regime shifts: estimated relationships degrade exactly when correlations spike in crises, and deleveraging events (e.g., August 2007 quant unwind) cause many stat-arb books to lose simultaneously.
misconceptions: That 'arbitrage' here means riskless profit; statistical arbitrage is a set of probabilistic bets that can and do produce extended losses.
example: A fund residuals-neutralizes 2,000 U.S. stocks against sector and style factors, shorts stocks 2 sigma above their model price, buys those 2 sigma below, and rebalances daily.

name: Convertible arbitrage
definition: A market-neutral hedge-fund strategy involving the simultaneous purchase of a convertible security (usually a convertible bond) and the short sale of the same issuer's common stock, designed to exploit inefficient pricing of the convertible relative to the underlying equity. The short stock position is sized to the convertible's equity sensitivity (delta), and the position is dynamically re-hedged.
intuition: Buy the convertible bond, short the stock against it: if the bond is cheap relative to the stock-plus-option it embeds, you harvest the difference while staying roughly immune to small stock moves.
mechanics: The arbitrageur buys the convertible and shorts a delta-neutral ratio of the underlying shares, capturing the bond's coupon plus the cheapness of the embedded equity option; as the stock moves, the hedge ratio is rebalanced (dynamic delta hedging), and this re-hedging of a long-gamma position adds to returns.
formula: Shares shorted = delta_cv x conversion ratio x number of bonds, where delta_cv is the sensitivity of the convertible's price to the underlying stock price.
failure_modes: Credit events hurt both legs at once (e.g., the 2005 GM downgrade: long convertibles lost on credit while short equity rallied); liquidity gaps can also make convertible prices fall faster than the stock hedge gains, as in 1987.
misconceptions: That the trade is riskless because it is hedged; it carries credit risk, liquidity risk, and model risk in the delta estimate, and returns depend heavily on cheap financing and borrow availability for the short leg.
example: A fund buys $10 million face of a convertible trading below theoretical value and shorts 60,000 shares of the issuer (the delta hedge), earning the coupon and gamma P&L as it re-hedges.

name: Fixed-income arbitrage
definition: A group of market-neutral strategies that exploit pricing differences between related fixed-income securities or contracts, such as swap-spread, yield-curve, mortgage, and cash-futures basis trades. Positions pair long and short exposures in economically similar instruments and bet on the convergence of small yield or price discrepancies, usually with substantial leverage.
intuition: Two bonds or rates that should be priced almost identically sometimes are not; fixed-income arbs buy the cheap one, short the rich one, and wait for the tiny gap to close.
mechanics: Traders identify rich/cheap points using yield-curve models, financing via repo; typical trades include long Treasury/short swap (swap-spread), butterfly structures on the curve, long MBS hedged with Treasuries or swaps, and long cash bond/short futures (basis). Returns per trade are small, so leverage is high.
formula: Swap spread = yield to maturity of the Treasury bond minus the fixed rate of the matched-maturity interest-rate swap (sign conventions vary by market).
failure_modes: High leverage on small spreads means liquidity and financing shocks force losses: the LTCM collapse (1998) and the March 2020 Treasury basis unwind show convergence trades diverging further before converging, triggering margin spirals.
misconceptions: That convergence is guaranteed within a tolerable horizon; 'riskless' relative-value trades can stay mispriced longer than a levered trader can stay solvent.
example: A desk buys the cheapest-to-deliver 10-year Treasury, shorts the matched futures contract, finances the bond in repo, and plans to hold the position as the basis converges toward delivery.

name: Volatility arbitrage
definition: A class of option-based relative-value strategies that trade the difference between an option's implied volatility and a forecast of the underlying's future realized volatility, implemented through a delta-neutral portfolio of options and the underlying. The trader treats volatility, rather than price, as the unit of relative value: buying options delta-hedged is a bet that realized volatility will exceed implied, and selling them is the opposite bet.
intuition: If the market is pricing options as if the stock will move 10% but you think it will move 20%, you can buy the options, hedge out the direction, and profit from the extra movement itself.
mechanics: Forecast realized volatility (e.g., from historical or high-frequency returns), compare with implied volatility backed out of market option prices, then buy underpriced or sell overpriced options and keep the book delta-neutral by trading the underlying. Profit is realized through the continuous re-hedging (gamma scalping) of the position over the option's life.
formula: Option value C = f(S, sigma, ...); implied volatility sigma_imp solves C_market = f(S, sigma_imp, ...). Trade long vol if sigma_imp < sigma_forecast, short vol if sigma_imp > sigma_forecast.
failure_modes: It is not true arbitrage: the forecast can be wrong, and volatility spikes correlated across markets (black-swan events) cause losses across a whole book, as with LTCM's short-volatility positions.
misconceptions: That delta-hedging removes all risk; a delta-neutral book still carries gamma, vega, theta, and jump risk, and 'buying vol cheap' loses steadily through theta if the realized move never comes.
example: A trader buys S&P 500 straddles at 12% implied volatility while forecasting 18% realized, delta-hedging daily; if realized vol comes in near 18%, the re-hedging gains exceed the theta paid.

name: Dispersion trading
definition: An options relative-value strategy that trades the spread between the implied volatility of an index and the implied volatilities of its constituent stocks. The classic construction is short index options (straddles or variance) against long options on the components - a position that profits when realized correlation comes in below the correlation embedded in index option prices.
intuition: Index option implied volatility embeds an average pairwise correlation among components; if the stocks move less in lockstep than implied, the index's realized volatility undershoots the volatility of its parts, rewarding the short-index/long-components book.
mechanics: Sell index options and buy options on index constituents in vega- or notional-weighted proportions, then delta-hedge both legs. P&L is driven by the gap between realized component volatilities and realized index volatility, which scales with realized correlation.
formula: sigma_index^2 approx sum(w_i^2 sigma_i^2) + 2 sum_{i<j}(w_i w_j rho_ij sigma_i sigma_j): index variance as a function of component weights w, volatilities sigma, and average correlation rho; dispersion trades short implied rho against expected realized rho.
failure_modes: A market crash drives realized correlation toward one, producing large losses for short-correlation books; the position also carries net short-volatility exposure, so implied-volatility spikes hurt even without a correlation shock.
misconceptions: That dispersion trading is a pure, hedged correlation bet; imperfect baskets and residual vega and skew exposures mean it is short crash risk, not riskless arbitrage.
example: A trader sells a 3-month at-the-money index straddle at 18% implied vol and buys straddles on the 20 largest components averaging 28% implied vol, delta-hedged daily; if realized correlation is 0.30 instead of the implied 0.55, index realized vol prints near 14% and the short index leg gains more than the long legs lose.

name: Gamma scalping
definition: A dynamic-hedging options strategy in which a trader holds a long-gamma options position (such as a straddle) and repeatedly rebalances an offsetting position in the underlying to keep the book delta-neutral, harvesting small gains from realized price oscillations. It monetizes the difference between realized volatility and the implied volatility paid for the options.
intuition: Being long gamma means your delta grows when the underlying rises and shrinks when it falls, so re-hedging mechanically forces you to sell high and buy low; if the underlying wiggles more than the implied volatility you paid for, the scalps can outearn the theta decay.
mechanics: Buy calls (short underlying) or puts (long underlying) in delta-matched size, then re-hedge as delta changes: sell the underlying as it rises and buy it as it falls. The book is net long gamma and short theta, so it profits only if realized volatility exceeds implied volatility net of hedging costs.
formula: Approximate hedging P&L = 0.5 x Gamma x S^2 x (sigma_realized^2 - sigma_implied^2) x t, minus transaction costs, where Gamma is position gamma and S the underlying price.
failure_modes: In quiet markets theta decay bleeds the position faster than scalps accumulate, and frequent re-hedging racks up commissions and slippage that can erase the theoretical volatility edge.
misconceptions: That gamma scalping is a directional strategy; it is explicitly non-directional and loses when the underlying trends smoothly without oscillation or sits still.
example: Buy 10 calls with delta 0.29 and gamma 0.005 for $12 each and short 290 shares; the stock rises $5, call delta becomes 0.32, so short 30 more shares at $480 and buy them back at $475 - a roughly $150 scalp set against daily theta decay.

name: Delta-neutral trading
definition: A portfolio construction approach that offsets positive and negative deltas so the combined position has near-zero sensitivity to small moves in the underlying's price. Directional risk is neutralized so that other exposures - volatility, time decay, or carry - drive the P&L.
intuition: If an option behaves like 40 shares, holding 40 offsetting shares cancels first-order price risk; what remains is the curvature (gamma), the clock (theta), and the volatility exposure (vega).
mechanics: Compute the net delta of all legs (option deltas summed per contract times multiplier; stock counts one per share) and trade the underlying to bring net delta to zero, rebalancing as prices, time, and implied volatility shift the Greeks.
formula: Delta_portfolio = sum(n_i x Delta_i) = 0, where n_i is the number of contracts or shares and Delta_i the per-unit delta of each leg.
failure_modes: Delta neutrality holds only for small moves: large gaps or volatility spikes change delta faster than rebalancing can track, and a perfectly delta-neutral book can still lose heavily through vega, theta, and funding costs.
misconceptions: That delta-neutral means risk-free; it only neutralizes first-order directional exposure, leaving convexity, volatility, and liquidity risks fully in place.
example: Long 10 puts with delta -0.31 plus long 310 shares gives net delta near zero; after a $1.24 drop the put delta moves to -0.43, so the trader buys 120 more shares to re-neutralize.

name: Market making
definition: A liquidity-provision activity in which a firm continuously quotes two-sided bid and ask prices, earning the spread (and any rebates) on turnover while managing the inventory risk of positions accumulated from filling customer orders. In U.S. equities, registered and off-exchange market makers also internalize a large share of retail order flow under Regulation NMS execution and disclosure rules.
intuition: The market maker is a dealer, not an investor: it tries to buy at the bid and sell at the offer thousands of times a day, and its enemy is holding inventory when prices move against it.
mechanics: Post limit orders on both sides around a fair-value estimate, adjust quotes as prices and inventory change, and hedge or internalize the resulting flow. The SEC's 2021 staff report describes how a small number of off-exchange market makers execute most individual-investor orders, with payment for order flow creating conflicts governed by best-execution and Rule 605/606 disclosure regimes.
failure_modes: Adverse selection - being run over by better-informed or faster flow - and inventory losses in one-way markets are the core failure modes; the January 2021 meme-stock episode forced extreme inventory and margin stress on off-exchange market makers.
misconceptions: That market making is riskless spread capture; losses on individual trades are routine and must be covered by aggregate spread income, and the economics depend on speed, rebates, and flow access unavailable to retail traders.
example: A market maker quotes a stock $50.00 bid / $50.02 offered, 1,000 shares up; it buys 500 at the bid and sells 500 at the offer for $10 gross, then hedges residual inventory when a news release moves fair value to $49.90.

name: Grid trading
definition: A systematic order-placement technique that lays a ladder of buy and sell orders at fixed price intervals above and below a reference price, harvesting oscillation or trend mechanically without forecasting direction. With-the-trend grids add exposure as price runs; against-the-trend (range) grids buy lower rungs and sell higher rungs to monetize mean reversion.
intuition: Instead of predicting where price will go, the grid turns the price axis into a conveyor belt: each step down triggers a buy and each step back up triggers a sell at the next rung, locking the spacing in as gross profit per completed cycle.
mechanics: Choose a base price, an interval (e.g., 10 pips), and a number of rungs, then place resting orders at each level. Range grids place buys below and sells above the base; trend grids do the reverse. Risk control requires a hard stop beyond the outermost rung, because position size grows against an adverse trend.
formula: Gross profit per completed grid cycle approx. grid interval x size per rung; with n rungs at spacing s around base P, orders sit at P +/- k*s for k = 1..n.
failure_modes: A sustained trend through the grid accumulates a large losing position (range grid) or forces profit give-back (trend grid); without a stop, a one-way move can exceed the sum of all harvested oscillation profits many times over.
misconceptions: That grid trading is a low-risk money machine because it wins frequently; the many small wins are paid for with an unbounded tail loss when price leaves the grid and never returns.
example: With EURUSD at 1.1450, place buys every 10 pips down to 1.1390 and sells every 10 pips up to 1.1510 with a stop at 1.1530; each completed down-up oscillation earns 10 pips per unit, while a run to 1.1530 stops the grid for a 270-pip worst case.

name: Dollar-cost averaging
definition: An accumulation strategy that invests a fixed dollar amount into an asset at regular intervals regardless of price, so that more units are bought when prices are low and fewer when prices are high. It replaces market-timing decisions with a mechanical purchase schedule.
intuition: A fixed $500 buys twice as many shares at $10 as at $20, so the average cost per share ends up below the average price over the period - the schedule does the buying-low work automatically.
mechanics: Divide the planned investment into equal tranches and deploy them on a fixed calendar (weekly, monthly, quarterly). Regulator education stresses that DCA changes when and how money is invested; it does not prevent losses or guarantee returns.
formula: Average cost per share = n x A / sum(A / P_i) = n / sum(1 / P_i), the harmonic mean of purchase prices P_i for fixed amount A per period.
failure_modes: In a steadily rising market DCA underperforms investing the lump sum up front because cash sits idle, and in a secular decline it systematically buys into losses; frequent small purchases can also carry proportionally high fees.
misconceptions: That DCA is a timing strategy that beats the market or removes risk; its benefit is behavioral discipline and timing-risk smoothing, and it still loses money in sustained downturns.
example: Investing $250 weekly into an ETF priced at $99, $96, $97, and $100 produces an average share cost of about $98.00, versus $99.00 for a week-one lump-sum purchase (CIRO illustration).

name: Value averaging
definition: An accumulation strategy, introduced by Michael Edleson in a 1988 AAII Journal article, in which the investor targets a fixed increase in the portfolio's total value each period (the value path) and invests or sells whatever amount is required to hit that target. Purchases are larger after declines and smaller - or negative - after rallies.
intuition: Dollar-cost averaging fixes the dollars you invest; value averaging fixes the growth of your portfolio's value, so the market itself dictates each installment - more when it is cheap, less, or even a sale, when it is rich.
mechanics: Set a target value for each period (e.g., initial amount plus $500 per month). At each rebalancing, compute the gap between the current holdings value and the target, then buy the shortfall or sell the excess. Required cash flows are unbounded, so reserves must be planned.
formula: Investment at period t = V_target(t) - (shares held x price_t), with V_target(t) = V_0 + t x deltaV for a linear value path.
failure_modes: Deep bear markets demand ever-larger purchases that can exceed available cash, and in taxable accounts the forced sales trigger capital-gains tax; the strategy also requires more monitoring and transactions than DCA.
misconceptions: That value averaging is strictly superior to DCA; its lower average cost comes from greater aggressiveness (larger investments after losses), which is a risk choice rather than a free lunch.
example: With a $500 monthly value path, a rally that lifts holdings $840 above target prompts a sale of about 7.3 shares ($340) instead of a purchase; a drop from $49.74 to $45.50 forces a $1,182 investment (AAII worked example).

name: Pyramiding
definition: A position-building tactic that adds to a winning trade in predefined increments as price moves in the position's favor, so that full size is carried only after the trade has proven itself. In trend systems the adds are mechanical - the Turtle rule adds one unit every 0.5N (half the average true range) above the previous fill.
intuition: Start small, let the market pay for confirmation, then press: each add is effectively financed by open profit, while stops trail so that the worst case on the full pyramid approximates the risk of the first unit.
mechanics: Define the initial unit, the add interval, and the maximum unit count before entry. Turtle construction: enter one unit at the breakout, add one unit per 0.5N advance up to four units, and raise stops on earlier units so total position risk stays near 2% of equity.
formula: Add price(k) = fill(k-1) + 0.5 x N for longs, where N is the 20-day exponential average true range; maximum four units in the Turtle system.
failure_modes: Late adds sit close to the reversal point, so a sharp give-back can turn a comfortably profitable trade into a scratch or a loss on the final units; in choppy, mean-reverting markets pyramids repeatedly stop out near the top of the range.
misconceptions: That pyramiding is the same as averaging down; pyramiding adds only to winners, while averaging down adds to losers - the two have opposite risk dynamics.
example: With N = 2.50 and a 55-day breakout at 310.00, buy units at 310.00, 311.25, 312.50, and 313.75, trailing the stop to 2N below the most recent fill (Turtle worked example).

name: Averaging down
definition: Adding to an existing long position as its price falls, which lowers the average cost per share and reduces the rebound needed to break even. It is a position-sizing practice rather than a complete strategy, most defensible within a valuation framework and strict risk limits.
intuition: Buying 100 shares at $50 and 100 more at $40 puts the cost basis at $45, so the position needs only a 12.5% recovery from $40 instead of a 25% one - but the investor now owns twice as much of a falling asset.
mechanics: Purchase additional shares at successively lower prices per a predetermined plan (fixed increments or valuation triggers). The new average cost is the share-weighted mean of purchase prices, and position size and portfolio concentration grow with each add.
formula: Average cost = sum(q_i x p_i) / sum(q_i) over all purchases i.
failure_modes: If the decline reflects deteriorating fundamentals rather than noise, averaging down concentrates the portfolio in a loser - the classic falling-knife path to outsized single-name losses.
misconceptions: That a lower average cost means lower risk; the break-even math improves but total capital at risk rises with every add, and the practice is often used to avoid admitting a mistake rather than as a rational plan.
example: 100 shares at $60 plus 100 more at $40 gives a $50 basis: the position needs only a 25% rise from $40 to profit instead of 50% - but $14,000 is now exposed to one stock.

name: Averaging up
definition: Buying additional shares of an existing position at successively higher prices, raising the average cost basis while increasing exposure to a rising asset. It is the mirror of averaging down and the discrete-time cousin of pyramiding into strength.
intuition: Leaning into winners trades a worse average price for a bigger position in a confirmed trend - you pay up precisely because the market is validating the thesis.
mechanics: Add tranches at predetermined higher price points or on technical triggers such as moving-average breaks or momentum readings. Each add raises the cost basis, so the position becomes increasingly sensitive to a reversal from the peak.
formula: Average cost = sum(q_i x p_i) / sum(q_i); equal buys at $20, $24, $28, and $32 give a $26 basis.
failure_modes: Buying into late-stage momentum risks adding just before exhaustion; a sharp reversal puts the later, higher-priced tranches underwater immediately, and rising concentration compounds the loss.
misconceptions: That averaging up is always reckless; disciplined versions predetermine add points and total size, whereas the undisciplined version is simply chasing. It is also distinct from dollar-cost averaging, which is price-agnostic rather than momentum-following.
example: Buying XYZ at $20 and then equal amounts at $24, $28, and $32 yields a $26 basis; a drop to $25 loses money on the whole position even though the first tranche is still up 25%.

name: Scaling in
definition: Building a position in multiple tranches at different prices instead of committing full size at once - either into weakness (lowering average cost) or into strength (adding as the trade proves itself). It spreads execution and timing risk and lets the trader confirm the thesis before full deployment.
intuition: Splitting a 1,000-share buy into four 250-share steps at descending prices turns one all-or-nothing decision into a graduated one, at the cost of sometimes never reaching full size.
mechanics: Set a target price and total size, then place partial orders at intervals, stopping when price reverses or full size is reached. Scaling in also reduces market impact and helps hide large orders; many traders start small and add only as the trade moves in their favor.
formula: Average entry = sum(q_i x p_i) / sum(q_i); four 250-share tranches at $20.00, $19.90, $19.80, $19.70 average $19.85.
failure_modes: Scaling into weakness means deliberately growing a losing position; if the thesis is wrong, the trader reaches maximum size at the point of maximum loss.
misconceptions: That scaling in always improves the entry; if price runs without filling the remaining rungs, the trader is underinvested in their best ideas - opportunity cost is the price of the smoother entry.
example: An investor wanting 1,000 shares of a $20 stock buys 250 shares each at $20.00, $19.90, $19.80, and $19.70, averaging $19.85 instead of $20.00 (Investopedia worked example).

name: Scaling out
definition: Closing a position in partial tranches at successively more favorable prices rather than exiting all at once, banking profits progressively while leaving a residual position to capture further movement.
intuition: Selling a third at each target converts an all-or-nothing exit into a ladder: some profit is locked in, and the remaining runner is effectively financed by realized gains.
mechanics: Predefine partial-exit levels or targets; as each is reached, close a fraction of the position and commonly move the stop on the remainder to break-even or better, so the residual position carries little remaining downside relative to the entry.
formula: Remaining size after k exits = Q_0 - sum(q_i); realized P&L = sum(q_i x (p_i - p_entry)) over exited tranches i.
failure_modes: In strong trends scaling out caps participation in the biggest moves - the residual runner earns a fraction of what full size would have; in choppy markets premature partials plus tightened stops can exit the whole position at the worst moments.
misconceptions: That scaling out is always the prudent choice; its main documented benefit is psychological and risk-smoothing, and fixed full exits can outperform staggered ones when trends persist.
example: Holding 900 shares from a $50 entry, sell 300 at $52 and 300 at $54, move the stop to $50, and let the last 300 run - $1,200 is banked while upside exposure remains.

name: Core-satellite approach
definition: A portfolio-construction framework that places the majority of assets in a low-cost, passively managed core tracking broad market indexes, surrounded by smaller actively managed satellite positions intended to add alpha or diversification. It blends passive efficiency with bounded active risk.
intuition: Lock in the market return on most of the money and confine your bets to a satellite sleeve, where manager skill or concentrated themes can only help or hurt at the margin.
mechanics: Allocate the core to index funds or ETFs (e.g., an S&P 500 tracker) and the satellites to active funds, sectors, or strategies (high-yield bonds, biotech, commodities), then rebalance to hold the split. The core minimizes costs and portfolio beta while satellites carry the tracking error.
failure_modes: Poor satellite selection or an excessive satellite weight erodes the cost and risk benefits, effectively recreating an expensive active portfolio; persistent active underperformance drags total return below the cheap index the core was meant to secure.
misconceptions: That the framework itself generates outperformance; it is an organizational discipline - the satellites still must earn their fees, and most active managers do not beat their benchmarks net of costs.
example: 50% in an S&P 500 index fund as the core, with 10% in an actively managed high-yield bond fund, 20% in a biotechnology fund, and 20% in a commodities fund as satellites (Investopedia illustration).

name: Buy and hold
definition: A passive investment strategy of purchasing securities - typically diversified equity funds - and holding them for years regardless of short-term price fluctuations, forgoing timing decisions in favor of long-run participation in asset growth. Positions are selected once and traded only for rebalancing, contributions, or withdrawals.
intuition: If you cannot reliably predict next month's price, own productive assets and let compounding and time in the market do the work; every round trip avoided is costs and taxes not paid.
mechanics: Acquire the chosen assets and hold through bull and bear markets; capital-gains taxes are deferred until sale, and turnover and transaction costs approach zero. Indexed implementations hold constituents as long as they remain in the index, with annual turnover often under 5%.
failure_modes: Secular bear markets or buying at extreme valuations can produce a decade or more of flat real returns, and behavioral failure - panic selling at the bottom - converts a temporary drawdown into a permanent loss.
misconceptions: That buy and hold means never reassessing; the strategy concerns trading frequency, not due diligence - holdings still require periodic review for thesis or allocation drift, and long-run equity outperformance is a historical pattern, not a law.
example: 100 shares of Apple bought at $18 in January 2008 and held to January 2019 (then $157) returned nearly 900% over 11 years without a single trade (Investopedia example).

name: Carry trade
definition: A strategy of funding in a low-interest-rate currency (or asset) and investing in a high-interest-rate one to earn the interest differential, in violation of the uncovered-interest-parity benchmark that predicts offsetting depreciation. Its return profile is short-volatility: steady differential income punctuated by crash risk on the investment currency.
intuition: Borrow yen at 0.5%, buy Australian dollars at 4.5%, and pocket the four-point spread - as long as AUD does not slide; the trade earns until everyone unwinds at once, which is why it goes up by the stairs and down by the elevator.
mechanics: Sell or borrow the funding currency and buy the investment currency via spot, forwards, or futures, holding the differential as carry. Brunnermeier, Nagel and Pedersen (2009) document that high interest differentials predict negative skewness: crashes cluster with funding-liquidity squeezes and VIX spikes, when speculators unwind positions.
formula: Carry return z(t+1) = (i*_t - i_t) - delta_s(t+1), where i* - i is the interest differential and delta_s the depreciation of the investment currency; profit requires the differential to exceed depreciation.
failure_modes: Funding-liquidity spirals force synchronized unwinds - investment currencies crash precisely when speculators must delever (e.g., the October 1998 dollar-yen collapse); rising global risk aversion (VIX, TED spread) is the canonical kill switch.
misconceptions: That the carry differential is riskless arbitrage; the average profit coexists with negative skewness, so the return is compensation for bearing crash risk rather than a free lunch.
example: A position long AUD funded in USD earned about the 0.6% quarterly differential plus 0.3% FX excess return in the 1986-2006 sample, while carrying average daily-return skewness around -0.32 (Brunnermeier-Nagel-Pedersen summary statistics).

citations.source: Brunnermeier, Nagel & Pedersen, 'Carry Trades and Currency Crashes', NBER Macroeconomics Annual 2008, vol. 23

name: Basis trade
definition: A relative-value strategy that trades the basis - the spread between an asset's cash (spot) price and its futures price - by going long the cheap leg and short the rich leg, expecting convergence as the futures contract approaches delivery. The position is neutral to the asset's outright price and earns or loses the change in the spread.
intuition: A futures contract and the deliverable asset are the same thing at expiry, so any gap between them today beyond financing and carry is a harvestable mispricing: buy the cheap one, sell the dear one, and wait for them to meet.
mechanics: Compute fair value (spot plus cost of carry minus income such as dividends) and compare it with the futures price; if futures are rich, buy the asset and short the futures (long the basis), financing the cash leg, then hold to convergence or roll. Index-arbitrage desks apply the same logic to index futures versus the constituent basket.
formula: Basis = futures price - spot price; fair value = cash x (1 + r x x/360) - dividends, so the tradeable edge approx. actual basis minus theoretical basis.
failure_modes: The basis can widen before it converges, forcing margin and financing stress on the leveraged position - the archetypal limit-to-arbitrage failure; funding-cost spikes and forced unwinds (March 2020 Treasuries) can turn a convergent trade into a large realized loss.
misconceptions: That basis trades are riskless arbitrage; convergence is only assured at delivery, and the leverage used to make thin spreads economical makes interim widening potentially fatal.
example: With the S&P future trading 8 points above fair value, a desk buys the 500-stock basket and shorts the future; as expiry approaches, the two converge and the desk captures the 8 points less financing and execution costs.

name: Cash-futures basis trade
definition: The Treasury-market instantiation of the basis trade: arbitrageurs, chiefly hedge funds, buy cash Treasury notes and bonds and short Treasury futures when futures trade above their no-arbitrage price, financing the bond in the repo market so the position requires almost no net cash outlay. Profit comes from cash and futures prices converging by the delivery date.
intuition: If the future is priced above what the deliverable bond plus financing costs, you can warehouse the bond, deliver into the future, and lock in the gap - as long as your repo funding survives until delivery.
mechanics: Identify the cheapest-to-deliver Treasury, buy it, short the corresponding CBOT futures contract, and finance the bond with overnight or short-term repo while posting futures margin. The Office of Financial Research estimates hedge-fund basis positions peaked around $400-500 billion before March 2020, when margin and repo stress forced partial unwinds.
formula: No-arbitrage condition: P(t,tau) = sum_s B(t,s) c_s + B(t,T) F(t,tau,T) - the cash bond price equals discounted coupons plus the discounted futures invoice price; violations define the tradeable disconnect.
failure_modes: Overnight repo creates rollover risk and futures margin creates cash-call risk; in March 2020 rising margins and repo costs forced hedge funds to sell the cash leg into an illiquid market, amplifying Treasury-market stress until the Federal Reserve intervened.
misconceptions: That the high leverage makes the trade speculative rather than arbitrage; the position is hedged against rate moves, and its fragility comes from funding structure, not directional exposure.
example: From end-2017 to September 2019 hedge-fund Treasury exposure roughly doubled to $2.02 trillion while short futures positions rose $352 billion - the footprint of the long-basis build-up that partially unwound in March 2020 (OFR estimates).

name: Funding-rate arbitrage
definition: A crypto-market cash-and-carry style strategy that pairs a position in a perpetual futures contract with the opposite position in spot to harvest the funding rate - the periodic payment exchanged between perp longs and shorts that tethers the contract to the index price. When funding is positive, the classic trade shorts the perp and holds spot, collecting funding from longs.
intuition: Perpetual futures never expire, so exchanges tax the crowded side: when longs pay shorts 0.01% every eight hours, being short the perp and long the coin collects the toll while the two legs' price risk cancels.
mechanics: Hold spot (or a margin-equivalent) against an equal-notional short perp; funding payments accrue to the short when the rate is positive (contango) and to the long when negative (backwardation), typically every eight hours. The position is directionally hedged; risks are funding-rate flips, borrow and margin costs, liquidation mechanics, and exchange counterparty risk.
formula: Funding payment per interval = position notional x funding rate; a $10,000 position at +0.01% pays or receives $1 every 8 hours.
failure_modes: Funding flips sign in sharp selloffs, turning the income stream into a cost, and adverse wicks can liquidate the leveraged leg before the spot leg can be unwound, breaking the hedge; exchange freezes or defaults are uncompensated tail risks.
misconceptions: That it is risk-free yield; the hedge is imperfect under liquidation and margin rules, and high positive funding usually signals crowded leverage that unwinds violently.
example: With BTC perp funding at +0.01% per 8 hours, short $100,000 of perp against $100,000 of spot and collect about $30 per day in funding while the legs' price P&L nets to zero - until funding flips negative.

name: Cross-exchange arbitrage
definition: Buying an asset on the exchange where it is cheaper and simultaneously selling it where it is dearer to capture the price gap between venues. In cryptocurrency markets, Makarov and Schoar (2020) document that such deviations are recurrent and much larger across countries than within them, reflecting capital controls and limits to arbitrage.
intuition: The same bitcoin should not be worth $30,000 in Seoul and $29,400 in New York for long - but moving dollars and coins across borders and exchanges is slow and costly, so the gap persists and pays whoever can bridge it.
mechanics: Monitor quoted prices across venues, buy on the cheap exchange and sell on the expensive one, then rebalance fiat and asset inventories between venues. Speed, transfer costs, withdrawal limits, and capital controls determine which gaps are actually capturable.
formula: Gross edge = P_venueB - P_venueA - (transfer + trading + FX costs); Makarov-Schoar find cross-country deviations co-move and widen during large bitcoin appreciations.
failure_modes: Transfer and settlement delays mean the legs are not simultaneous in practice - the gap can close while assets are in transit, and withdrawal halts, capital controls, or counterparty failure can strand one leg entirely.
misconceptions: That a visible price gap equals capturable profit; the documented gaps persist precisely because frictions - capital controls and slow-moving arbitrage capital - prevent most traders from closing them.
example: Bitcoin trades $500 higher on a Korean exchange than a U.S. one; an arbitrageur buys in the U.S. and sells in Korea but captures the spread only after moving won proceeds back through the banking system - days of exposure, not milliseconds.

name: Latency arbitrage
definition: A high-frequency strategy that exploits the mechanical arbitrage opportunities created when correlated securities' prices update at slightly different times across venues, racing to trade on a stale quote before its owner can update it. Budish, Cramton and Shim (2015) show this arms race is built into the continuous limit order book design itself.
intuition: When the E-mini jumps in Chicago, the SPY quote in New York is wrong for a few milliseconds; being first to pick off that stale quote is worth millions a year, so firms spend hundreds of millions on being microseconds faster.
mechanics: Colocate near exchange matching engines, consume direct feeds, and send orders against quotes that have not yet incorporated price moves in correlated instruments. BCS document ES-SPY correlation falling to about 0.09 at 10 milliseconds and 0.007 at 1 millisecond, with the median arbitrage duration shrinking from 97ms in 2005 to 7ms in 2011 while profit per opportunity stayed roughly constant.
formula: Median ES-SPY arbitrage profit approx. 0.08 index points per unit, about 1,000 opportunities per day (roughly $75 million per year) in the BCS 2005-2011 sample.
failure_modes: The rent is competed away in speed rather than in price: as rivals get faster, capture requires ever-larger infrastructure spending for the same prize, and market-design changes such as frequent batch auctions or speed bumps can eliminate the opportunity set outright.
misconceptions: That latency arbitrage involves predicting prices; it exploits purely mechanical, publicly visible mispricings whose existence depends on serial processing in continuous markets, not on information or forecasting skill.
example: At 1:51:39.590 pm the E-mini jumps about 2.5 index points while SPY has not yet reacted; the fastest firm buys SPY at the stale offer and unwinds moments later at the corrected price, capturing the spread (BCS Figure 1.1 example).

name: Index arbitrage
definition: A strategy that exploits deviations between the price of an index futures contract (or ETF) and the theoretical fair value of the underlying constituent basket, buying the cheaper side and selling the richer. It is the engine of classic program trading and enforces the law of one price between index derivatives and their components.
intuition: The S&P 500 future is just the 500 stocks in a wrapper; if the wrapper trades rich to the contents, sell the wrapper and buy the contents - computers do this in milliseconds, which is why the gap rarely exceeds transaction costs.
mechanics: Compute fair value = cash index x (1 + r x x/360) - dividends and compare it with the futures price; beyond a threshold set by round-trip costs, execute the basket and the futures as a unit. Opportunities are fleeting and razor-thin, so the strategy is dominated by institutions with high-speed execution and near-zero costs.
formula: Fair value = cash x {1 + r(x/360)} - dividends; trade triggers when |futures - fair value| > round-trip transaction costs.
failure_modes: Execution-leg risk: a 500-stock basket cannot be filled at the quoted snapshot, so slippage can consume the edge; in dislocations (e.g., August 24, 2015) constituent and ETF prices detach violently, and part of the apparent gap is unpriceable, illiquid components.
misconceptions: That index arbitrage is accessible to retail traders; the capital, speed, and cost structure needed to profit from sub-0.1% discrepancies are institutional by construction.
example: If S&P 500 futures trade 0.2% above fair value, an institution buys all 500 stocks in index weights and shorts the equivalent futures, unwinding both at convergence for the spread minus financing and costs.

name: Calendar arbitrage
definition: Trading the price relationship between futures (or options) on the same underlying with different expiration months - the intra-commodity calendar spread - by buying one expiry and selling another to capture changes in the term-structure gap rather than the outright price. Framed as arbitrage, it targets spreads that deviate from carry-implied or historical norms.
intuition: March wheat and September wheat are the same wheat at different dates; the gap between them reflects storage, financing, and seasonal demand - trade the gap when it stretches beyond what carry justifies.
mechanics: Buy the nearby (or deferred) month and sell the other as a single unit with two legs; P&L equals the change in the inter-month spread. Exchanges grant reduced margins on calendar spreads because systematic market risk largely nets out between the legs.
formula: Spread P&L = (P_near,exit - P_near,entry) - (P_far,exit - P_far,entry); a spread narrowing from -11 to -8 cents on a 5,000-bushel wheat contract earns $150.
failure_modes: Spreads are not bounded by delivery the way cash-futures convergence is: supply shocks, delivery squeezes in the nearby month, or storage-regime changes can run the spread far past fair carry, and liquidity in the deferred leg can be thin.
misconceptions: That calendar spreads are slow and safe; nearby-month squeezes can move the spread more violently than the outright market, and the arbitrage framing is relative-value, not riskless.
example: Buy March wheat at 526'6 and sell September at 537'6 (spread -11'0); when the spread narrows to -8'0, the 3-cent gain on the 5,000-bushel contract is $150 (Investopedia worked example).

name: News trading
definition: A short-horizon style that trades the price impact of scheduled announcements (earnings, central-bank decisions, economic data) and unscheduled events, entering just before or immediately after the release to capture the volatility burst. Most news traders operate intraday, since the exploitable reaction is typically short-lived.
intuition: News is the one scheduled source of volatility: everyone knows when the payrolls print lands, nobody knows its content - the game is positioning for, reacting to, or fading the crowd's reaction better than the crowd.
mechanics: Prepare scenarios and alerts around the economic calendar; trade the initial directional reaction, the buy-the-rumor-sell-the-news unwind, or the fade once enthusiasm peaks. Stops must accommodate post-release volatility, and spread widening and slippage around releases are structural costs.
failure_modes: Spreads widen and liquidity vanishes exactly at the release, so theoretical fills are unavailable, and algorithmic reaction times leave discretionary traders structurally late; fading a genuinely regime-changing headline is a standing source of large losses.
misconceptions: That knowing the news content is the edge; prices react to the surprise relative to expectations, not the headline itself - a good number can sell the asset off if it was not good enough.
example: A trader shorts EUR/USD strength minutes after a payrolls beat that fell short of the whisper number, covering an hour later as the initial dollar spike fades.

name: Earnings trading
definition: Trading equity positions around quarterly earnings announcements to exploit the announcement-day volatility and the post-announcement price drift documented in the accounting literature. Implementations range from intraday reaction trades to holding surprise winners and losers for the multi-week drift.
intuition: Earnings are scheduled surprises: prices jump at the print and then, on average, keep crawling in the direction of the surprise for weeks, as if the market digests the news only gradually.
mechanics: Screen for upcoming reports, estimate the surprise (actual versus consensus), and trade the direction of the surprise or the subsequent drift. Bernard and Thomas (1989) document post-earnings-announcement drift: abnormal returns continue in the direction of the surprise for roughly 60 days, a pattern they find consistent with delayed price response rather than risk mismeasurement.
formula: Surprise proxies include SUE = (EPS_actual - EPS_expected) / sigma(forecast errors); portfolios sorted on SUE show drift in cumulative abnormal returns over the following quarter.
failure_modes: Announcement windows concentrate gap risk - positions held through the print face binary moves that jump stops - and crowding plus post-publication decay of the drift anomaly compress the available edge.
misconceptions: That earnings trading is just guessing the number; systematic versions trade the market's reaction function (surprise to drift), not the fundamental outcome itself.
example: A stock reports EPS 15% above consensus and gaps up 6% at the open; a drift-following position held for the following weeks targets the continuation documented beyond the initial jump.

name: Opening-range breakout
definition: An intraday strategy that marks the high and low of the session's first minutes (commonly the first 15) and enters in the direction of a break beyond that range, treating the opening battle as the day's reference for momentum. It is a named day-trading system without a canonical academic source.
intuition: The first 15 minutes concentrate overnight information and the day's heaviest volume; whichever side wins that skirmish often keeps control, so the range edges become the day's natural trigger levels.
mechanics: Mark the opening-range high and low; enter long on a break above the high or short below the low, with stops inside the range or below the breakout candle and targets as multiples of risk or of the range width. The day's high or low is printed in the opening minutes far more often than a random walk would imply.
formula: Long trigger: price > opening-range high; risk unit = OR high minus stop; a common first target is entry + 2 x risk unit.
failure_modes: False breakouts in mean-reverting sessions stop the trade repeatedly, and on low-conviction range-bound days the OR edges are noise rather than information; slippage at the open is structurally high.
misconceptions: That every opening-range break is tradable; practitioners filter by gap context, relative volume, and higher-timeframe trend - the raw breakout is an analytical framework, not a validated edge.
example: With a stock's 15-minute opening range at $41.08-$41.65, a break above $41.65 at 9:55 a.m. triggers a long with a stop below $41.08 and a first target near $42.80 (about 2R).

citations.source: Investopedia, 'Guide to Using the Opening Range in Trading'

name: Gap-and-go strategy
definition: A day-trading momentum strategy that buys (or shorts) a stock that gaps at the open on high volume and continues trending in the gap direction without a meaningful pullback, entering on continuation beyond the opening range. It is a named practitioner setup with no canonical source.
intuition: A high-volume gap means overnight information repriced the stock and trapped the other side; if price never looks back, the trapped traders' exits and momentum chasers feed a one-way move you ride with tight invalidation.
mechanics: Screen for gaps with elevated premarket and opening volume; enter on the break of the opening range in the gap direction, place the stop at the prior session's close or the gap's far edge, and trail the exit with a trend line or the most recent swing low.
failure_modes: The setup's evil twin is the gap fade: gaps that stall and fill trap momentum entries at the day's extreme, and wide opening spreads plus slippage make realized entries far worse than chart-based backtests suggest.
misconceptions: That the gap direction is itself the signal; practitioners require volume confirmation and continuation structure - many gaps fill, and trading every gap is an exercise in chasing.
example: A stock gaps up 8% on earnings with triple normal opening volume; the trader buys the break of the first 5-minute high, stops below the prior close, and exits when the rising trend line from the open is breached near midday.

name: Fade strategy
definition: A contrarian tactic that trades against the prevailing move - selling into strength or buying into weakness - on the premise that the late stages of a move are driven by slow-reacting traders and prone to reversal. Common applications include fading overextended intraday moves and fading the initial reaction to economic data releases.
intuition: If everyone who wanted to buy has already bought, the marginal flow runs out and the move stalls; fading is selling the exhaustion of a crowded move rather than its beginning.
mechanics: Identify an extended move (a news spike, vertical run, or stretched deviation from a reference), enter against it with a defined invalidation beyond the extreme, and target reversion toward the pre-move level or a mean. Fading economic releases typically waits for the first reaction to complete before entering against it, with wider stops to survive post-release volatility.
failure_modes: Trends persist far beyond apparent exhaustion, so fading strong trends produces repeated losses punctuated by occasional large ones when the trader averages into the fade; on regime-changing news the reversal simply never comes.
misconceptions: That fading is synonymous with recklessness; disciplined fades use the same invalidation-first construction as any other setup, but it is a regime-dependent framework rather than a validated general edge.
example: After a payrolls beat sends USD/JPY up 80 pips in minutes, a fade trader sells the pair once momentum stalls, targeting a retrace of half the spike with a stop above the reaction high.

name: Pairs spread z-score strategy
definition: A statistical-arbitrage rule that monitors the spread between two historically linked securities, standardizes it as a z-score against its own rolling mean and standard deviation, and enters a market-neutral long/short when the spread stretches beyond a threshold (commonly two standard deviations), exiting at reversion. It is the standardized-distance variant of the Gatev-Goetzmann-Rouwenhorst pairs rule.
intuition: If two stocks usually move together, the times they do not are opportunities: when the gap is two standard deviations wide, history says it more often narrows than widens - so you short the leader and buy the laggard.
mechanics: Estimate the spread (price ratio or hedge-ratio residual), compute z = (spread - rolling mean) / rolling sigma, open the pair when |z| exceeds the entry threshold, and close when z reverts toward zero or crosses the exit threshold. Gatev et al. (2006) match pairs by minimum distance between normalized price series and trade divergences beyond two historical standard deviations.
formula: z_t = (s_t - mu_s) / sigma_s; enter short the spread if z_t > +2, long if z_t < -2, exit near z_t approx. 0.
failure_modes: Structural breaks - a takeover, earnings regime change, or delisting - turn a stretched spread into a permanently repriced one while the z-score keeps signaling reversion, and rolling-window estimates degrade in volatility regime shifts.
misconceptions: That a 2-sigma threshold makes the trade statistically safe; spread distributions are fat-tailed and non-stationary, so extreme readings cluster exactly when the pair relationship is breaking.
example: Two retail stocks' price-ratio spread has mean 1.00 and sigma 0.02; when the spread hits 1.05 (z = 2.5), short the outperformer and buy the underperformer dollar-neutral, exiting when the spread returns to 1.01.

citations.source: Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst, 'Pairs Trading: Performance of a Relative Value Arbitrage Rule' (SSRN; published RFS 2006)

name: Channel breakout strategy
definition: A trend-entry rule that buys when price exceeds the highest high (or sells when it breaks the lowest low) of a trailing N-period channel, on the premise that a break of an established range marks the start of a sustained move. It is the 'trading range break' rule tested by Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron (1992) and generalized in Donchian-style systems.
intuition: A market coiled in a box stores energy; a break beyond the box means buyers or sellers finally overwhelmed the range boundary, and the absence of nearby reference points lets the move run.
mechanics: Compute the channel as the rolling N-day high and low; enter long one tick above the N-day high or short one tick below the N-day low, with stops inside the prior range or ATR-based. Brock-Lakonishok-LeBaron tested trading-range-break rules on the Dow from 1897 to 1986, finding buy and sell signals asymmetric in return and volatility relative to random-walk, AR(1), GARCH-M, and EGARCH nulls.
formula: Long signal: P_t > max(H over t-N..t-1); short signal: P_t < min(L over t-N..t-1).
failure_modes: Sideways, mean-reverting markets generate repeated false breakouts whose accumulated small losses define the strategy's cost; the rule is structurally many small losers against few big winners, so choppy regimes bleed it.
misconceptions: That the channel length is the secret; results are far more sensitive to regime, costs, and exit rules than to the exact lookback, and the academic evidence is descriptive of historical data rather than a proven predictive law.
example: With a 50-day high at $102, a stop-entry buy triggers at $102.05; the protective stop sits at the 10-day low of $96, risking about 6% of price on the position.

citations.source: Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron, 'Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns', Journal of Finance 47(5), 1992, 1731-1764 (EconPapers record)

name: Moving-average crossover strategy
definition: A trend-following rule that goes long when a short moving average crosses above a longer one and exits or shorts on the reverse cross, using the smoothed momentum of two lookback windows as the signal. It is the canonical moving-average rule in Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron's (1992) tests of simple technical trading rules.
intuition: The short average is the market's recent mood, the long average its season; when mood crosses season something has changed - you trade the crossing, accepting that you will be late at both turns.
mechanics: Compute a fast and a slow moving average; hold long while the fast average is above the slow one (golden-cross state) and flat or short while below (death-cross state), optionally with a band filter to suppress noise crosses. Brock-Lakonishok-LeBaron tested variable-length moving-average rules (e.g., 1/50, 1/150, 5/150, 1/200, 2/200) on the Dow from 1897 to 1986 with bootstrap comparisons.
formula: SMA_N(t) = (1/N) sum_{i=0}^{N-1} P(t-i); signal = sign(SMA_fast - SMA_slow).
failure_modes: In range-bound markets the crossovers whipsaw, entering at local extremes of each oscillation, and the rule's structural lag means V-shaped reversals cost the full round trip before the signal flips.
misconceptions: That a golden cross is a validated buy signal; it is a descriptive trend-following framework whose historical test results are sample- and cost-dependent, not a proven predictive law.
example: A 50-day SMA rising through the 200-day SMA at $98 flips the system long; it stays long until the 50-day falls back below the 200-day at $91, capturing the intervening trend less the lag at both ends.

citations.source: Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron, 'Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns', Journal of Finance 47(5), 1992, 1731-1764 (EconPapers record)

name: Donchian breakout strategy
definition: A channel-breakout system built on Donchian channels - the trailing N-day high and low - entering long when price exceeds the channel top and short when it breaks the channel bottom, most famously as the 20-day (System 1) and 55-day (System 2) entries of the Turtle rules. Exits use a shorter opposite channel: 10-day for System 1 and 20-day for System 2.
intuition: Richard Donchian's insight was that you need not predict trends, only agree to join every new N-day extreme; most breakouts fail, but the few that run pay for all of them.
mechanics: Enter one unit when price trades one tick beyond the 20-day high or low (System 1, skipped if the previous breakout was a winner, with a 55-day failsafe entry) or the 55-day high or low (System 2, all taken). Stop at 2N, add units every 0.5N, and exit on the opposite 10-day (System 1) or 20-day (System 2) extreme.
formula: Upper channel = max(high, last 20 or 55 days); lower channel = min(low, last 20 or 55 days); N = 20-day exponential average of True Range, used for sizing and stops.
failure_modes: Long flat or choppy stretches produce strings of losing false breakouts, and because entries sit at the extreme, slippage and stop-outs cluster at the worst prices; whatever edge exists lives entirely in rare, fat-tailed trends.
misconceptions: That the 20/55 parameters are magic; the Turtles themselves emphasized N-based position sizing and consistency over the entry parameters, which any similar channel length approximates.
example: Gold's 55-day high is 310.00 with N = 2.50: buy one unit at 310.00, add at 311.25, 312.50, and 313.75, stop the pyramid 2N below the last fill, and exit on a 20-day low (Turtle worked example).

citations.source: Curtis Faith, 'The Original Turtle Trading Rules' (originalturtles.org, 2003)

name: Turtle trading
definition: The complete mechanical trend-following system Richard Dennis and William Eckhardt taught their 'Turtle' trainees in 1983-84: Donchian-channel breakout entries, volatility-normalized position sizing in units of 1% risk per N, 2N stops, adds every 0.5N, and portfolio-level unit limits. Published in full by original Turtle Curtis Faith as 'The Original Turtle Trading Rules' (2003).
intuition: Dennis's bet was that trading could be taught as rules: trade many liquid futures markets, risk a fixed volatility fraction per unit, take every breakout, and let a few giant trends pay for dozens of stopped-out false starts.
mechanics: N is the 20-day exponential average of True Range; unit size = 1% of account / (N x dollars per point). System 1 enters on 20-day breakouts (skipped after a winning breakout, with a 55-day failsafe), System 2 on 55-day breakouts (all taken). Stops sit 2N from entry (about 2% risk); add one unit per 0.5N up to four; unit caps are 4 per market, 6 in closely correlated markets, 10 in loosely correlated, and 12 per direction; exits are 10-day (System 1) or 20-day (System 2) opposite extremes.
formula: Unit = (0.01 x account equity) / (N x dollars per point); N_t = (19 x N_{t-1} + TR_t) / 20, where TR is the daily true range.
failure_modes: Trend following fails in long trendless regimes: strings of 2N stop-outs grind equity down, and the published, widely copied rules invite crowded entries and slippage at exactly the breakout points; the system's own rule of cutting account size 20% after each 10% loss exists because losing streaks are the norm.
misconceptions: That the entry signals were the secret; Dennis held the rules could be printed in a newspaper because consistency, discipline, and N-based sizing were the real edge - and historical success is not a promise of profitability in today's markets.
example: On a $1,000,000 account with heating-oil N = 0.0141 and $42,000 per point, one unit = $10,000 / $592.20, truncated to 16 contracts; a 20-day breakout buys one unit with a stop 2N away, risking about 2% of equity (Turtle rules worked example).

citations.source: Curtis Faith, 'The Original Turtle Trading Rules' (originalturtles.org, 2003)
