name: Risk-on risk-off trading
definition: A macro positioning framework that rotates between higher-risk assets (equities, cyclicals, commodities, credit) in optimistic risk-on regimes and safe havens (Treasuries, gold, cash, reserve currencies) in fearful risk-off regimes, driven by shifts in aggregate investor risk tolerance. The correlated cross-asset moves in these regimes are the phenomenon the framework trades.
intuition: In RORO markets the global portfolio breathes as one organism: when fear rises, everything risky is sold together and everything safe is bought together, so the trade is the regime, not the asset.
mechanics: Define regime indicators (equity momentum, credit spreads, volatility indexes, dollar strength) and shift allocations or take paired positions - long equities against short Treasuries in risk-on, the reverse in risk-off. Dedicated products such as RORO ETFs mechanize the rotation between high-risk equities and low-risk Treasuries.
failure_modes: Regime labels are obvious only in hindsight; choppy transitions whipsaw rotation signals, and structural shifts - such as stock-bond correlation turning positive in inflation regimes - break the canonical risk-on/risk-off pairings.
misconceptions: That risk-off means all risky assets fall and all havens rise every day; RORO describes correlation tendencies in aggregate risk appetite, not a daily law, and idiosyncratic news routinely overrides it.
example: When weak data and falling earnings guidance flip the indicators risk-off, a rotation fund shifts from 80% equities / 20% Treasuries to 30% / 70%, cutting drawdown if the selloff continues but forfeiting the rebound if it does not.

name: Global macro trading
definition: A top-down strategy class that takes long and short positions across equity indexes, government bonds, currencies, and commodities based on macroeconomic and political analysis - interest-rate paths, growth differentials, policy shifts, and geopolitics. It is practiced by global macro hedge funds in discretionary, systematic, and CTA forms.
intuition: Instead of asking which stock is cheap, ask which country's whole story is mispriced - then express the view with the most efficient instrument: its currency, its bonds, its equity index, or its commodities.
mechanics: Build theses from rates, growth, government policy, and geopolitics, then express them via liquid instruments - FX forwards, sovereign bond futures, equity index futures, and options - often with leverage. Sub-strategies are typically currency-based, interest-rate-based, or equity-index-based; CTA and systematic funds implement model-driven, frequently trend-following versions.
failure_modes: Macro theses fail on timing: a correct long-run view can bleed carry and mark-to-market losses for years before paying - or never pay - and policy surprises such as central-bank pivots or capital controls gap markets against leveraged books.
misconceptions: That global macro is glorified forecasting; practitioners emphasize asymmetric expression (options, defined-risk structures) and risk budgeting over point predictions, and the label covers both discretionary judgment and fully systematic models, which behave very differently.
example: A manager bearish on U.S. growth shorts S&P 500 futures and goes long 10-year Treasury futures, while going long the currency of a commodity exporter whose terms of trade are improving.

name: Relative strength rotation
definition: A cross-sectional allocation strategy that periodically rotates capital into the assets, sectors, or industries with the strongest recent relative performance and out of the weakest, harvesting the momentum effect at the group level. It operationalizes industry momentum, which Moskowitz and Grinblatt (1999) showed accounts for much of individual-stock momentum.
intuition: Leadership persists longer than contrarians expect: the sectors that led last quarter tend to keep leading next quarter, so you systematically climb aboard the leaders and abandon the laggards on a fixed schedule.
mechanics: Rank candidates (sectors, industries, or asset classes) by trailing 3- to 12-month total return, hold the top ranks - or go long the top group and short the bottom - and re-rank and rebalance monthly or quarterly. Moskowitz-Grinblatt find industry momentum significant even after controlling for size, book-to-market, individual-stock momentum, and microstructure effects.
formula: Score_i = R_i(t-12, t-1) (optionally skipping the most recent month); hold the top-k candidates by score.
failure_modes: Momentum crashes - sharp reversals after crises - rotate leadership violently, so the strategy buys the old leaders just as they mean-revert; high turnover also makes costs and taxes a first-order drag.
misconceptions: That relative strength is a chart heuristic; the academic version is a systematic cross-sectional ranking with a documented but decaying, crash-prone return pattern, and the rotation adds nothing if the ranking window is noise.
example: Each month, rank 11 sector ETFs by trailing 6-month return, hold the top 3 equal-weighted, and rotate; in a year where energy leads technology by 25 points, the portfolio stays long energy until its rank decays.

citations.source: Moskowitz & Grinblatt, 'Do Industries Explain Momentum?', Journal of Finance 54(4), 1999, 1249-1290 (EconPapers record)

name: Cross-sectional momentum
definition: The anomaly and strategy class of buying securities with the highest recent returns relative to their peers and selling those with the lowest, over 3- to 12-month formation and holding periods. Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) documented that such relative-strength portfolios generated significant abnormal returns not explained by systematic risk or delayed reaction to common factors.
intuition: Winners keep winning and losers keep losing for a while: rank the whole market by recent performance, buy the top decile, short the bottom, and let the persistence work over the next quarter.
mechanics: Each month, rank stocks by past J-month return (J = 3-12), form decile portfolios, buy the top decile and short the bottom, and hold for K months (K = 3-12) with overlapping monthly cohorts. Jegadeesh-Titman found the strongest strategies earning roughly 1% per month in 1965-1989 data, with part of the first-year abnormal return dissipating over the following two years.
formula: Momentum return = R(top decile by past J-month return) - R(bottom decile), measured over holding period K and averaged across overlapping (J,K) cohorts.
failure_modes: Momentum crashes - violent reversals concentrated in rebound phases after market declines - can erase years of gains in months, and turnover plus short-side costs are large; the published anomaly has decayed as it became crowded.
misconceptions: That it is a free lunch refuting market efficiency; subsequent literature ties the premium to crash risk, behavioral underreaction, and trading costs - it is a risky, capacity-constrained anomaly, not an arbitrage.
example: Rank 3,000 stocks by trailing 6-month return, buy the top 300 and short the bottom 300, hold 3 months, and reform monthly; Jegadeesh-Titman's tests show the best such zero-cost portfolios averaging about 1% per month before costs.

citations.source: Jegadeesh & Titman, 'Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers: Implications for Stock Market Efficiency', Journal of Finance 48(1), 1993, 65-91 (EconPapers record)

name: Time-series momentum
definition: A strategy that takes long positions in assets whose own trailing return is positive and short positions where it is negative - each asset against its own history rather than against peers - typically with volatility-scaled sizing. Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen (2012) document significant time-series momentum across 58 liquid futures in equity indexes, currencies, commodities, and bonds, persisting about a year and partially reversing thereafter.
intuition: Do not ask whether gold beat stocks; ask whether gold beat gold - if its own past year is up, be long, if down, be short, and size each bet so every market contributes equal risk.
mechanics: For each instrument, take the sign of the past 12-month excess return as the direction (long if positive, short if negative), size positions inversely to ex-ante volatility (estimated from exponentially weighted squared daily returns with a 60-day center of mass), and hold one month, averaging returns across cohorts. The diversified factor has little exposure to standard asset-pricing factors and performs best during extreme markets.
formula: Per-instrument TSMOM return = sign(r_{t-12..t-1}) x (40% / sigma_{t-1}) x r_t, with sigma^2 = 261 x sum_i (1-delta) delta^i (r_{t-1-i} - r_bar)^2.
failure_modes: Whipsawing ranges reverse the sign of trailing returns repeatedly, and sharp V-shaped reversals hit the strategy exactly when it is maximally positioned for the prior trend; crowding among trend-following funds compresses the effect out of sample.
misconceptions: That it is the same thing as cross-sectional momentum; time-series momentum uses an asset's own past return with no winner/loser ranking, and empirically it largely subsumes the cross-sectional stock effect while remaining a distinct construction.
example: Crude oil's trailing 12-month excess return is +18% with ex-ante volatility of 30%: go long sized at 40%/30% = 1.33 volatility units; natural gas at 60% volatility gets half that size, so both positions contribute equal risk.

citations.source: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen, 'Time Series Momentum', Journal of Financial Economics 104(2), 2012, 228-250 (author-hosted PDF, NYU Stern)

name: Post-earnings announcement drift
definition: The documented tendency of stock prices to continue moving in the direction of an earnings surprise for weeks after the announcement, and the strategy of trading that continuation. Bernard and Thomas (1989) showed cumulative abnormal returns drift with the sign of the surprise for roughly 60 days, concluding the pattern is consistent with a delayed price response rather than risk mismeasurement.
intuition: The market under-reacts to earnings: the announcement-day jump is only part of the move, so buying after good news - late, after everyone saw the print - historically still captured the slow digestion that followed.
mechanics: Rank announcements by standardized unexpected earnings or the announcement-window abnormal return; buy the highest-surprise decile and short the lowest, holding for the following weeks to a quarter. The effect is stronger for small companies and coexists with elevated announcement-period volatility.
formula: SUE = (EPS_actual - EPS_expected) / sigma(EPS forecast errors); portfolios sorted on SUE show cumulative abnormal return drift over the subsequent ~60 trading days.
failure_modes: The anomaly weakens as it is arbitraged and can invert in high-attention, high-liquidity names where reaction is instant; trading costs and the need to act immediately after each announcement consume much of the gross drift.
misconceptions: That PEAD guarantees upside after every earnings beat; it is a statistical tendency across large samples of announcements with wide dispersion - individual prints reverse violently all the time.
example: Buy the decile of stocks with the largest positive earnings surprises the day after reporting and short the most negative decile; Bernard-Thomas's sample shows the long-short portfolio continuing to earn abnormal returns over the following ~60 days.

citations.source: Bernard & Thomas, 'Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift: Delayed Price Response or Risk Premium?', Journal of Accounting Research 27 (1989), 1-36 (EconPapers record)

name: Short squeeze trading
definition: Trading that exploits the feedback loop in heavily shorted stocks, where rising prices force short sellers to buy shares to cover, pushing prices higher still and forcing further covering. Squeeze traders position long in high-short-interest names ahead of or during such cascades - a volatility event trade, not a valuation strategy.
intuition: Every short seller is a future guaranteed buyer; when the price rises enough that their losses force buying, the squeeze feeds on itself as the available float shrinks exactly when demand explodes.
mechanics: Screen for high short interest (percentage of float, days-to-cover), borrow-fee rates, and crowding; enter long on the triggering momentum and exit as covering exhausts. The SEC's 2021 staff report documents the GameStop episode: large short interest, surging individual-investor volume, price moves that forced covering, and resulting broker trading restrictions.
formula: Days to cover = short interest / average daily volume; squeeze risk rises with short interest as a percentage of float and with borrow cost.
failure_modes: Timing is everything: high short interest can persist for months while the stock bleeds lower, and late entries after the squeeze peak catch the collapse when covering ends and price returns toward fundamentals; trading halts and broker restrictions, as in January 2021, can trap positions entirely.
misconceptions: That a short squeeze reflects improving fundamentals; the SEC staff report attributes the GameStop price action to volume, sentiment, and covering dynamics rather than any change in the company's earnings prospects.
example: GameStop ran from $17.25 to a pre-market peak above $500 in January 2021 as shorts covered into rising prices, with cumulative short-seller losses estimated at about $5 billion and several brokers restricting purchases at the peak.

citations.source: U.S. SEC, Staff Report on Equity and Options Market Structure Conditions in Early 2021

name: Long squeeze trading
definition: Trading around the downside mirror of a short squeeze: sharp price declines that force leveraged or stop-protected long holders to sell, whose selling pressures more longs into selling and accelerates the drop. The trade either shorts into the cascade or buys the capitulation once forced selling exhausts.
intuition: Crowded longs with stops at the same levels are dominoes: the first forced sales hit the next stops, and a normal dip becomes an air pocket - the squeeze trader profits from the mechanics of others' exits.
mechanics: Identify crowded long positioning (high leverage, clustered stop levels, recent parabolic gains); short the breakdown through the stop cluster, or wait for the volume-spike capitulation and buy the reversion. Long squeezes are typically shorter and shallower than short squeezes because falling prices eventually meet value buyers.
failure_modes: Dips driven by long liquidations are indistinguishable from the start of genuine downtrends until afterward; buying capitulation in a real repricing is catching a falling knife, and shorting the breakdown risks immediate reversion once the shallow stop pool is cleared.
misconceptions: That every sharp down-move is a long squeeze to be bought; the term describes a specific forced-selling feedback loop, and without evidence of clustered leverage there is no mechanical reason to expect a bounce.
example: After a vertical run, a stock breaks a level dense with retail stops and drops 4% in minutes on huge volume with no news; the squeeze buyer waits for the volume climax, enters, and exits on the 2% snapback as forced selling dries up.

name: Pairs convergence trade
definition: The core pairs-trading position: when the spread between two historically co-moving securities diverges beyond a threshold, short the outperformer and buy the underperformer in expectation that the spread converges back to its historical relation. Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst (2006) formalized the rule, matching pairs by minimum distance between normalized price series and trading divergences beyond two standard deviations.
intuition: Two near-substitute stocks cannot stay mispriced relative to each other forever; the convergence trade sells whichever got too expensive and buys whichever got too cheap, hedging out the market's direction.
mechanics: Form pairs by minimum distance over a 12-month formation period; open when the normalized-price spread exceeds two historical standard deviations, and close on convergence, at the next formation date, or if the pair ceases to trade. Positions are dollar-neutral across the two legs, and a portfolio diversifies across many pairs.
formula: Open when |spread of normalized prices| > 2 sigma (historical); P&L approx. (converged spread - entry spread) per dollar-neutral unit.
failure_modes: Convergence fails when the divergence is informational - a takeover rumor, fraud, or fundamental break re-prices one leg permanently and the spread widens through every reversion threshold; Gatev et al. themselves document declining profitability as the strategy crowded.
misconceptions: That matched pairs make the trade market-neutral and therefore safe; neutrality holds only for the common factor - idiosyncratic divergence risk is the whole position, and it is fat-tailed.
example: Two beverage stocks' normalized prices separate by 2.5 standard deviations; short the leader and buy the laggard dollar-neutral, then unwind for a profit when the spread closes to 0.3 standard deviations three weeks later.

citations.source: Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst, 'Pairs Trading: Performance of a Relative Value Arbitrage Rule' (SSRN; published RFS 2006)

name: Pairs divergence trade
definition: The entry logic of a pairs trade: positioning as the spread between two linked securities diverges to an extreme, on the expectation that the divergence has run its course and the spread will close. In the Gatev-Goetzmann-Rouwenhorst framework, divergence beyond two historical standard deviations is precisely the event that triggers the dollar-neutral position.
intuition: Divergence is the signal, not the enemy: you wait for the rubber band between two stocks to stretch beyond historical tolerance, then take the position that profits as it snaps back.
mechanics: During the trading period, monitor the normalized-price spread of a formed pair; a divergence beyond +/-2 historical standard deviations opens the dollar-neutral long/short. Risk management defines a maximum adverse divergence (stop), because spreads can widen arbitrarily before closing - or never close.
formula: Trigger: |s_t| > 2 sigma_s, where s is the normalized price spread; position = short the high leg, long the low leg, in equal dollar amounts.
failure_modes: The central risk is divergence that never closes: structural breaks turn the entry signal into a trap, and each unit added to a widening spread increases exposure exactly as the probability of a permanent break rises.
misconceptions: That larger divergence means a better trade; beyond some point, extreme divergence correlates with pair breakdown (for example, an impending acquisition of one leg), so the biggest apparent opportunities carry the highest breakdown risk.
example: A pair's spread widens from 0 to -2.2 sigma over two weeks on no news; the trader buys the lagging leg and shorts the leader, with a stop at -3.5 sigma in case the relationship has broken.

citations.source: Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst, 'Pairs Trading: Performance of a Relative Value Arbitrage Rule' (SSRN; published RFS 2006)
